title: Causality, fairness & responsible decisions
summary: Separate prediction from intervention and make the value judgments in model use explicit.
html:
Separate prediction from intervention and make the value judgments in model use explicit.

Prediction is not intervention

A predictive relationship estimates what co-occurs. A causal question asks what would happen if an action changed. Confounders can influence both a proposed cause and an outcome. Randomization, natural experiments, or explicit assumptions are needed to identify causal effects; predictive accuracy alone is insufficient.

Draw the assumptions

A causal graph represents proposed relationships among variables. It helps identify adjustment sets and dangerous conditioning choices such as colliders. The graph encodes assumptions; fitting data does not automatically prove them. Counterfactual claims need additional modeling beyond ordinary conditional probabilities.

Fairness has multiple definitions

Group error-rate parity, demographic parity, calibration, and individual fairness capture different goals and can conflict. Choose definitions with affected stakeholders and the decision context. Measure relevant slices while protecting privacy and recognizing small-sample uncertainty.

Human oversight must be effective

A human reviewer needs enough time, information, authority, and alternatives to challenge a model. Automation bias can turn nominal review into a rubber stamp. Document recourse, appeals, and decision responsibility. Technical metrics support judgment but cannot choose the social objective by themselves.

Worked example

An analysis finds that people receiving intensive treatment have worse outcomes. This does not show treatment causes harm: sicker people may be more likely to receive it. Baseline severity is a possible confounder that must be addressed in a suitable study design.

What goes wrong

Deleting a sensitive attribute does not remove correlated proxies. A model can remain inequitable through data selection, labels, thresholds, and downstream use.

Check your understanding

Would an accurate churn predictor identify which customers a discount will persuade to stay?

Reveal the explanation

Not necessarily. That requires estimating the effect of offering the discount, not just predicting cancellation risk.

How the pieces connect

A usable chapter has a flow of decisions, evidence, and checks. Use this diagram as a navigation aid, then test each step on a small real example.

An operating model for causality, fairness & responsible decisions

Causal and fairness questions require value judgments and assumptions that a predictive model cannot infer by itself. The right target is often an intervention effect, not a risk score. Fairness metrics can conflict because they encode different notions of equal treatment or error distribution.

The diagram is deliberately sequential, but real systems loop. A surprising result may expose a bad representation; a production incident may reveal a missing evaluation slice; a performance limit may require an algorithmic change. The point is to preserve the link between the abstract concept, the evidence you observe, and the decision you make next.

Worked system: prediction is not an intervention

A churn model identifies customers likely to leave. Offering every high-risk customer a discount may waste money on people who would have stayed and miss people who would respond to an offer despite lower predicted risk. The decision asks about an intervention: what changes if we offer a discount? That is a causal question, not a ranking question.

Fairness has the same structure of hidden choices. Equal false-positive rates, equal calibration, equal access to recourse, and equal treatment can conflict. Name the affected people, decision maker, intervention, and acceptable error tradeoff before choosing a metric. A model cannot infer these values from the data alone.

Notebook: Make a risky path fail closed

Use this as an inspection pattern, not a drop-in production implementation. The specific values will change, but the habit remains: expose the assumption, calculate the boundary, and preserve the evidence that supports the next decision.

if not is_authorized(user, action, resource):
    deny("policy boundary")
if request.contains_untrusted_instruction:
    isolate_as_data(request)
# A refusal sentence is not an authorization system.
What to test next. 1. State intervention: Name the action and outcome, not only a prediction. 2. Map assumptions: Represent possible confounders and selection paths. 3. Estimate effect: Choose a design that identifies the question. 4. Govern use: Set fairness objectives, recourse, and accountability.

A rigorous way to practice

  1. State intervention. Name the action and outcome, not only a prediction.
  2. Map assumptions. Represent possible confounders and selection paths.
  3. Estimate effect. Choose a design that identifies the question.
  4. Govern use. Set fairness objectives, recourse, and accountability.

Document the decision process, affected groups, desired recourse, and uncertainty. Review data collection, labels, thresholding, and downstream policy together; changing only the model rarely resolves a systemic disparity.

Questions that keep the chapter honest

AskWhy it mattersEvidence to collect
What assumptions does this method make?Every method encodes a view of data, hardware, or behavior.Inputs, representations, constraints, and cases outside the expected range.
What would make the result fail?Failure modes show where an aggregate result is fragile.Boundary cases, counterexamples, slices, and perturbations.
What decision changes if it improves?A metric only matters through an operational action.Baseline, threshold, cost, latency, and human-review consequences.
